1:
Chrysostom explains the turn: having corrected the three heaviest charges, the distraction of the Church, the fornicator and the covetous man, Paul now uses a milder speech and interposes advice about marriage and virginity, whereas in the second epistle he ends with the more distressing matters. Barnes marks the same division formally, since the chapter begins the second part of the epistle, the discussion of points submitted in a letter from the church which has since been lost. Gill notes that for all the influence of the false apostles many at Corinth still corresponded with Paul, and that the questions may be collected from the chapter itself; Calvin adds that their consulting him shows they retained some respect for him, though what they asked is uncertain except so far as the reply discloses it.

What the opening verdict concedes is disputed. Robertson answers that the first question is whether a single life is wrong, and that Paul pointedly says it is not wrong but good, though a mark of certain heretics will be the forbidding to marry. Wesley reads it of the man who is master of himself, so great and many being the advantages of a single life. Henry limits the good to that juncture of time at least, denying that it means what is so conformable to the will of God that to do otherwise were sin. Calvin turns it against a later abuse, that soon after the first rise of the Church there crept in by Satan's artifice a superstition which, through a foolish admiration of celibacy, despised marriage. Lightfoot sets the verse against the rabbinic rule instead, where marriage is enjoined under a severe command laid on the man and not the woman, so that by exceeding twenty he makes an affirmative precept void.

On the reason given for marrying the commentators are anxious not to be misread. Ellicott renders it because of the prevalent fornication, so general at Corinth and so little accounted sin that the unmarried were liable to be led into it, and concedes that the apostle may seem to put marriage on merely utilitarian ground, answering that he writes with a limited aim. Robertson says the same more bluntly, that this is not the only reason for marriage though it is a true one, the main purpose being children and mutual love another. Calvin restricts the command, since the statement, universal as it sounds, belongs to those urged by necessity, every man judging for himself, while those who have the gift of abstinence are left at liberty. Barnes adds that Paul would keep the church from scandal, Gill that the advice prevents unlawful commerce of every kind, Clarke that Hosea uses the word of married people threatened with the loss of children, and Wesley that the words his own wife exclude polygamy.

Over the duty itself Gill observes that the Syriac renders the word due love, taking in all the offices of tenderness and care, though the phrase is here a euphemism for the marriage duty proper. Barnes praises its delicacy, the expression being removed as far as possible from the grossness of heathen writers, the word denoting kindness and good-will while the word due recalls the sacredness of the vow. Clarke calls it the matrimonial debt and warns that where it is withheld alienation of affection follows, which has in numberless cases led to adulterous connections. Calvin lays down the general doctrine of mutual benevolence and asks why the apostle levels husband and wife here instead of requiring obedience of the wife; Robertson answers that in wedlock separate ownership of the person ceases, and that this dictum defends marital intercourse against rigorists as the first verse commends celibacy against sensualists. Ellicott, citing Bengel, finds an elegant paradox in the saying that she has not power of her own body, and Wesley bids no one forget it on pretence of greater purity.
5:
Gill calls the withholding a piece of injustice and properly a defrauding, since both have a right to it, though under the conditions named it may be lawful to lie apart. Barnes insists that even by mutual consent the separation must not be perpetual, since that would expose them to the very evils marriage was designed to avoid; Clarke, that the separations permitted, for Paul enjoins none, are only for a season. Wesley makes the occasions special and solemn ones of devotion, and warns that if they remain long apart Satan will tempt them to unclean thoughts if not actions. Robertson notes that the verb means to have leisure, from the noun that gives us our word school, and that the tense makes it a single act and not a settled condition; the clause about the tempter is a present subjunctive, that Satan may not keep on tempting them.

Ellicott turns the verse into a piece of textual history. The alteration of the Greek verb into the present tense, so as to make the prayer refer to daily devotions rather than to special seasons, together with the interpolation of the word fasting, which the older manuscripts lack, he calls a striking example of the way the ascetic tendencies of one school of churchmen led them to amend the sacred text. Calvin defends the plainness of the passage from the other side: Paul was under necessity, knowing how much a false appearance of sanctity can beguile devout minds, since Satan dazzles us with a show of what is right until we imagine ourselves polluted by our own wives and think of leaving our calling.

What the permission covers is disputed. Barnes admits that it is uncertain whether the word refers back or forward, and that while the more natural construction looks backward, recent writers refer it forward and Calvin to the opening verse. Gill excludes the two things that are commands, that every man should have his own wife and that husband and wife should render what is due, and refers the permission to their parting for a time and coming together again; Wesley says the same. Ellicott would render it, I say this as a permission and not as a command, and warns that the English might seem to make the apostle claim only a permission to write: his meaning is that the foregoing instructions are not absolute commands but general permissive instruction, to be applied by each according to circumstances. Robertson glosses the noun as knowing together, understanding, and so concession, and concludes that Paul has not commanded people to marry but left it open.

On the wish that all were as he is, the commentators agree in narrowing it. Gill says Paul speaks not of his own state, which is uncertain, but of the gift of continency, desired for all that they may be fitter for the service of Christ. Barnes denies that he would prefer all men unmarried, which would be against the divine institution and his own precepts elsewhere, and makes the wish one for self-command like his own. Ellicott puts it as a wish that all had the same grace of continence, so that they might remain unmarried without risk of sin, God having given each man his own gift. Clarke ties the wish to the present distress, since Paul could never wish that marriage should cease among men or that the Church should always be composed of single persons. Calvin concludes that had this passage been duly weighed, the perverse superstition attached to the desire of celibacy, which is the root and cause of great evils, would never have gained a footing in the world; and Wesley, who thinks Paul had tasted the sweetness of that liberty and wished others to enjoy it, ends where our Lord ended, that all men cannot receive this saying save those to whom it is given.
8:
Who is addressed comes first. Gill takes the unmarried for those who never married or those whose wives are dead, preferring the second because widows are joined with them. Barnes allows the word either sense and says it means those then unmarried, the reasoning applying to both, widows being named where widowers are not because the never-married are treated later. Ellicott explains the pairing as a precaution, lest a question arise whether the advice was meant for widows at all; Robertson thinks it possible that only men are meant, virgins being treated separately later.

From that the old question follows. Clarke holds that the apostle speaks of men once married and now widowers, and that in saying even as I he means he was one himself, several of the ancients ranking Paul among the married apostles. Ellicott calls the conjecture, which Luther among others made, a curious one: it requires the word unmarried to be restricted to widowers, which is quite inadmissible, and even then the deduction could scarcely be called logical, the almost universal tradition of the early Church being that Paul was never married. Robertson agrees that it is hardly likely Paul means only widowers and widows and means to call himself a widower. Wesley holds that Paul was then single beyond doubt and that the history makes it probable he always was, and that the declaration has no reference to persecution.

Calvin ties the advice to what precedes: the gifts of God are variously distributed and continency is not in every man's power, so that an unmarried life ought to be desired by those who can bear it, each measuring himself by his own measure. At the next words he turns sharply. While he advises abstinence Paul always speaks conditionally, but where the infirmity of the flesh will not allow that liberty he enjoins marriage as a thing not in the least doubtful, so that no one may take it for mere advice; nor is it only fornicators that he restrains but those defiled in the sight of God by inward lust, and a man who neglects the remedy tempts God, so that the matter requires not advice but strict prohibition. Robertson notes that Paul has nowhere said celibacy is better than marriage, though he has justified it; Ellicott puts the ground of the comparison plainly, that to be influenced by unlawful desire is a sin while to marry is none. Gill draws the corollary that second marriages are lawful, which some of the ancients condemned, and Cyril of Jerusalem says as much, that those who marry but once should not reprobate those who consent to a second, since continence is noble and yet a second marriage is permissible, that the weak may not fall into fornication.

What the burning means divides them. Clarke reports Bishop Pearce's rendering, that it is better to marry than to be made uneasy, the verb meaning primarily to burn but metaphorically to be troubled; he denies that Paul can mean burning with lust, any more than Virgil does in saying that the unfortunate Dido burns. Gill takes it of the fire of lust itself, neither material fire nor the hell fire such uncleanness deserves. Barnes says the passion is often compared to a fire and that it is better to marry, with all the inconveniences of married life in a time of persecution, than to be the prey of raging passions; Robertson, that the metaphorical use is common enough, for grief as well. Calvin denies that there is strictly a comparison here, marriage being lawful while the other thing is exceedingly wrong. Lightfoot supplies a rabbinic story of a man who adjured the evil affection to go out of him, whereupon it went out as a pillar of fire, and who said to it, Thou art fire and I am flesh, yet for all that I have prevailed against thee.
10:
Gill marks the change of footing: to the unmarried Paul spoke by permission, but to the married what he says is by commandment, enjoining what they are bound to observe. What the disclaimer means is the question. Ellicott denies that the contrast is between Paul as an inspired apostle and Paul as a private man, since he claims elsewhere that all his apostolic commands are the commandments of the Lord. Robertson gives the plain account: Paul had no word of Jesus about the unmarried, but Jesus had spoken to the married, and Paul here reinforces his own inspired command by the Master's. Clarke says he gives no private opinion, since the Lord Jesus has commanded that man shall not put asunder what God has joined; Wesley reads it as not I only but Christ by his express command; Barnes insists that it is not advice but a solemn divine command. Lightfoot sets it beside the distinction usual in the rabbinic schools between producing a text of Scripture and producing an opinion.

Henry supplies the occasion. The question, frequent in that age and especially among Jewish converts, was whether they were to live with heathen relatives in a married state, since the law of Moses permitted divorce and there was a famous instance when the people were obliged to put away their idolatrous wives; this might well raise a scruple whether converts were not bound to desert mates who continued unbelieving. To that the apostle answers in general that marriage by Christ's command is for life, so that those who are married must not think of separation. Clarke fills in the Jewish background, where the marriage bond was held very loosely, and among the Jews the wife had as much right to put away her husband as he to put away her, which served as a mutual check.

Calvin takes the verse for the indissolubility of the tie and finds in it a condemnation of all those divorces which were of daily occurrence among the heathen and went unpunished among the Jews. He is surprised that no exception is made even for adultery, since Paul is not likely to have meant to curtail the doctrine of Christ, and concludes that, writing of these matters in passing, the apostle chose rather to send the Corinthians back to the Lord's own words. At the next verse he adds that what is said cannot apply to those put away for adultery, as the punishment shows, that being a capital crime by the Roman law; what he has in view is husbands who divorced their wives because their manners were not congenial or their appearance did not please, and wives who deserted their husbands for cruelty, and against all such he holds that marriage is not dissolved by divorces or dissensions. Clarke agrees that divorces cannot be allowed but in the case of fornication, which alone dissolves the vow; Wesley excepts the same cause, and Gill says the departure supposed is not thereby allowed.

On what follows a separation already made the readings converge. Ellicott renders it, if she have actually separated, and treats the clause as a parenthesis, the Lord's command being completed only by the words about the husband; the apostle anticipates the hard case by noting that such a woman must not marry again but ought to be reunited to her former husband. Barnes supposes the rule aimed at wives who, ignorant of Christ's rule and supposing they had a right to separate, had rashly done so and thought the contract dissolved: they must either be reconciled or remain alone, the tie being too sacred to be broken by either party's will. Robertson observes that Paul makes no allowance here for the remarriage of the innocent party, as Jesus does by implication, and glosses the verb for being reconciled as an old compound for exchanging coins of equal value.
12:
Ellicott marks the new class: up to this point only Christians have been in view, and there remains the case of mixed marriages, of which Corinth must have had many; the words are emphatically of a man who already has a wife, a Christian's marrying a heathen being forbidden elsewhere. Gill explains it the same way, that what went before was addressed to those on equal footing in religion, whereas here the apostle gives his own sense under inspiration, no express determination of the Lord's being extant. Robertson denies that it disclaims inspiration, since Paul means only that he is not quoting a command of Jesus; the problem is new, thrown up by the work among the Gentiles, so that Paul deals with mixed marriages as missionaries do now. Wesley calls it revelation from God though our Lord left no commandment on the point, and Calvin insists that what is Paul's is not therefore not the Lord's.

Calvin sets out the answer in two clauses: the believer ought not to withdraw or seek a divorce unless put away, and if an unbeliever puts away a spouse on account of religion the believer is by that rejection freed from the bond. Clarke puts the first rule plainly, that the husband is not to put his wife away because she continues in her heathen superstition; Wesley meets the obvious precedent, that the Jews were of old obliged to put away their idolatrous wives, but their case differed, since they were forbidden to marry such women while these married when both were heathen. Ellicott notes that the same strong verb is used of the woman as of the man, since under Roman law a wife could equally obtain a divorce, and rejects the suggestion that it is chosen because her being a Christian makes her the superior. Barnes reads the change of phrase practically, since the wife had no power to expel her husband from his own house though she might think separation her duty; she should rather love him and seek his welfare, that she may win him.

The scruple is met head on. Calvin states it fully: the relationship is so close that it seems impossible for a believer to live with an ungodly spouse without pollution; Paul declares nevertheless that marriage is sacred and pure and that no contagion need be feared, though he speaks not of contracting such marriages but of maintaining those already contracted. Barnes frames the objection as a question, whether one is not defiled by a close union with an enemy of the gospel, and answers that the contrary may be true. Clarke would render it that the unbeliever is to be reputed as sanctified on account of the believing spouse, her sanctity in outward things being imputed to him so as to make the connection not unlawful, the word applying to the Christian state rather than to any moral change. Ellicott sets this lawful union against that other in which the connection is defiling, and holds that the purity of the believing partner entirely overweighs the impurity of the unbeliever, which is ceremonial rather than moral. Robertson is blunter: Paul does not mean the unbelieving husband is saved by his wife's faith, though Hodge actually so interprets him, but only that the marriage relation is sanctified so that no divorce is needed.

The children settle it. Robertson supplies the ellipsis, that since it is otherwise your children are illegitimate; Ellicott says the children of such marriages were reckoned Christian children, and that the fruit being holy we must regard the tree as holy too, though the holiness meant is not that inward sanctification which springs from faith. Wesley makes the argument an appeal to sight, since otherwise the children would have been brought up heathens, whereas now they are Christians. Gill notes that the better reading is by the believing wife.
15:
Gill defines the case: the unbelieving party separates on account of religion and in hatred of it, refusing to live with the believer unless Christ is denied and his worship relinquished. Ellicott puts it as a question of conscience, since where the married life is made intolerable by the unbeliever urging religious acts conscience cannot approve, the earlier commands for continued union do not hold; and the permission is in no way contrary to our Lord's single ground of divorce, the apostle having reminded his readers that the Lord's command does not cover this case. Barnes says shortly that you cannot prevent it and must bear it patiently as a Christian. Calvin makes the ground stronger still: the unbeliever who repudiates a spouse ready to dwell with them makes a divorce with God rather than with the partner, so that here the first and chief bond is not merely loosed but utterly broken through.

How far the liberty extends is the old question. Barnes reports that many have supposed the deserted party free to marry again, Calvin, Grotius and Rosenmuller among them, but holds it contrary to the strain of the argument, the sense being that the one left is not bound to make provision for the one who departed. Clarke reads it as freedom from any particular laws preventing remarriage, and thinks the law probably stood so then though it does not now, since marriage can be dissolved only by death or by the ecclesiastical court, and neither adultery nor an obstinate separation gives the abandoned party authority to remarry. Robertson holds that wilful desertion sets the other free, a case not contemplated in Christ's words, and notes that Luther argued the released partner might marry again, which is by no means clear unless the unbeliever marries first. Wesley says only that the believer is at full liberty, and takes the next clause as a charge to live peaceably with them if possible; Robertson glosses the same words as a permanent call in the sphere of peace.

What the last verse of the section does is disputed as sharply. Calvin takes it as an exhortation drawn from the advantage to be gained, since it is a great blessing if a wife win her husband, and unbelievers are not so hopeless that they cannot be brought to believe, being dead indeed but not beyond the God who raises the dead; so long as any hope of doing good remains the pious wife should not go. Barnes reads it the same way, as a reason why the believing party should not separate needlessly, the probability of the other's conversion being reason enough for continuing together. Clarke turns it into direct counsel, that Christians with heathen partners should not give them up but bear their cross and look to God, who may give the unbelieving husband or wife to their prayers.

Ellicott reverses the whole reading. The verse has generally been taken as modifying what precedes, as though the apostle advised against letting the unbeliever go wherever there was any chance of a conversion; but the true meaning, he holds, is precisely the opposite, since so remote a contingency is too vague a thing for which to risk the peace that is an essential element of the Christian life. Robertson concedes that the syntax allows either construction and that the second suits the context best and is adopted by most commentators, while confessing that he hesitates to read Paul as favouring divorce unless the unbeliever insists, since there is no problem unless the unbeliever makes one, and where the case is hopeless acquiescence is the only wise solution. Gill offers both senses without deciding, the first being that the believer may be easy at the departure, there being no certainty of doing the other any good.
17:
Ellicott treats the intervening question as a parenthesis, so that this rule follows straight on the permission and limits the very broad liberty just granted: there the unbelieving partner alone is spoken of as acting, the believer merely acquiescing for peace and never promoting a separation. Robertson says the same, that the verse states the general principle which settles these questions and is illustrated afterwards by circumcision and slavery, so that while there is to be no compulsory bondage between believer and pagan there is to be no reckless abuse of the liberty either. Gill notices that the words look both ways, back to every man's proper gift and forward to what follows. Clarke reads the closing clause as a disclaimer of favouritism, since Paul lays on them no burden that others are not called to bear but a general rule imposed on every Christian society.

Henry takes the principle at its widest: our states and circumstances in this world are distributions of divine Providence, which fixes the bounds of men's habitations and orders their steps, God setting up and pulling down; and whatever a man's condition was when converted, let him abide in it. Calvin makes contentment the substance of it, that every one should be satisfied with his calling and pursue it instead of betaking himself to something else, a calling in Scripture meaning a lawful mode of life related to the God who calls us to it. Clarke adds that any situation of life is equally friendly to the salvation of the soul if a man is faithful to the grace received, so that a Christian should be content in all; Wesley, that he should not change his outward state without a clear direction from Providence.

Over the word itself Ellicott dissents from them all. Calling must not be taken in the modern sense of a profession or condition in life, since it is nowhere so used in the New Testament but always signifies God's calling of us: the charge is to continue Christians of the kind God's call made you. Barnes goes the other way and supposes the English use of the word for a profession arose from the belief that God calls every man to the rank he occupies, so that each has a call to his trade as really as a minister has to his. Gill glosses it as the civil calling and station of life, Wesley as the outward state.

The illustrations follow. Barnes explains that the removal of the marks of circumcision was often attempted by men ashamed of it, a practice Jewish writers describe; Clarke adds that it could be done by art and that Celsus prescribes the mode. Robertson states the point plainly, that a Jew is to remain a Jew and a Gentile a Gentile, both on an equality in the churches, and that this freedom illustrates the freedom about mixed marriages. Lightfoot supplies a stranger fact from the rabbins, that some Jews always went uncircumcised, and that uncircumcised priests ministered at the altar without complaint and indeed without fault, which the fathers of the traditions themselves confess. Ellicott warns that those who count a ceremony unimportant often magnify the disregard of it into a virtue, against which the apostle guards by declaring both conditions nothing, and points to the circumcising of Timothy and the refusal to circumcise Titus as illustrations of the rule and of Paul's own adherence to it. Calvin thinks the example designedly chosen to reprove in passing the superstition and haughtiness of the Jews, since men who gloried in circumcision might well be dissatisfied without it, so that Paul levels both conditions lest through hatred of the one the other be foolishly desired. Gill allows that circumcision was once a command and a type while denying it any place in justification; Barnes, Clarke and Wesley agree that keeping the commandments is the whole matter.
21:
Barnes sets the scale of the question, since slaves abounded in Greece and in every part of the heathen world. Ellicott renders the opening as a question about the past, whether a man was called while a slave, and answers that slavery does not affect the completeness of his conversion, so that he need feel no anxiety to escape it. Calvin says the apostle's object is to satisfy their consciences, exhorting servants to be of good cheer and not cast down as though servitude hindered them in serving God, and to be content rather than concerned how to throw off the yoke. Robertson notes that slavery was usually a fixed condition and a slave could be a good servant of Christ even under a heathen master; on the permission that follows he points out that there is no pronoun in the Greek at all and asks what is to be supplied, answering that freedom is the natural word. Clarke and Wesley take it the same way, that a man should prefer liberty for the temporal advantages that go with it and embrace the opportunity when it comes.

The paradox that follows is read as consolation and as check. Ellicott renders it that the man converted as a slave is Christ's freedman while the man converted free is Christ's slave, and distinguishes a freedman from a freeman as one who has been in bondage and is now out of it. Robertson explains the word as an old term for a manumitted slave, Christ having paid the ransom of his own life and being the patron to whom the freedman owes everything. Barnes makes it a delicate and happy argument to reconcile the slave to his condition, the bondage he has been freed from being far more grievous than the one he is in. Calvin sees the two halves working opposite ways, the one alleviating the bitterness of servitude, the other restraining the free-born lest they be unduly elated.

What the prohibition means divides them. Robertson takes it at its widest and finds here Paul's clear opposition to human slavery as an institution, which comes out so powerfully in the letter to Philemon. Calvin narrows it to obedience, since servants are to take heed not to subject themselves to the depraved inclinations of their masters, being holy to the Lord who redeemed them and not to defile themselves for the sake of men. Barnes makes it a matter of self-regard, that even in that relation they are to think of themselves as serving God. Clarke reports the interrogative rendering, whether they were bought out of slavery, and the counsel never to sell themselves again. Lightfoot asks whether the apostle speaks the words as his own sense or puts them as an objection which he answers next, and recalls that the Jews objected in just this way on the strength of the liberty obtained in the redemption out of Egypt, refusing to be called anything but free.

Clarke suspects that some Corinthian slaves had concluded that their Christian privileges absolved them from continuing slaves, a spirit which would soon have bred insubordination and scandal. Calvin guards the rule from the other side, that men are not bound by a perpetual necessity so as never to change their condition if a fit occasion offers, the apostle repressing only those thoughtless humours which hurry men hither and thither. Gill notes that the address as brethren is meant to engage them, since whatever the difference in their civil state there was none in their religious one. Wesley reads the closing charge as doing all unto God and in his immediate presence, so that those who abide with him keep a holy indifference about outward things; Robertson finds its comfort in a phrase, that even a slave can have God at his side by remaining at God's side.
25:
Gill and Barnes agree that a fresh question from the Corinthian letter is being taken up here, whether the unmarried should continue as they are. Barnes calls it the third subject on which Paul's opinion seems to have been asked, whether those with unmarried daughters or wards should give them in marriage, and suspects two grounds: that persecution made a family an added care, and that some at Corinth were already advocates of celibacy as the more pious state. Ellicott likewise makes it a new subject, the duty of parents regarding their young unmarried daughters, running to the end of the section. Clarke widens the word: though we take it of a pure unmarried young woman, it is evident that here it means young unmarried persons of either sex, citing Suidas on Abel, a virgin and a righteous man; Wesley says the same, of either sex. Robertson holds the narrower sense, young unmarried women only. Calvin takes the term as virginity itself, and says the apostle now returns to the marriage he began with, stating more explicitly what he had touched on obscurely.

The disclaimer is handled carefully by all of them. Robertson observes that Paul did have a command from the Lord earlier in the chapter, and that it was quite possible for him to know sayings of Jesus passed on among the believers even without access to a written gospel, but on virgins he had no specific word; what he gives instead is a deliberately formed decision, not a passing fancy, and the language about obtained mercy, far from disclaiming inspiration, expressly claims help from the Lord. Ellicott insists the contrast is not between Paul inspired and Paul uninspired but between Paul quoting the words of Christ and Paul instructing as an apostle. Calvin says the Lord nowhere declares who ought to remain unmarried, and that since male and female were created together the Scripture rather seems to call all indiscriminately to marriage; the word Paul uses signifies not merely advice but a decisive judgment, and the papists infer wrongly from it that one may go beyond the limits of God's word. Henry reads it as no express and universal law concerning celibacy but the judgment of one who had obtained mercy to be faithful, namely in the apostleship, faithfulness in the ministry being owing to the grace of Christ. Barnes says the advice of such a man, with no selfish end to gratify, is entitled to deference even where no explicit command is claimed.

On the reason given, the distress, Clarke defines the word as necessity, distress, tribulation, calamity, and pictures a man with a family at the mercy of enemies, the state often itself among the persecutors, when it would be far easier to provide for his own safety alone. Barnes takes it of trials then pressing, and adds the caution that Paul by no means meant this to be a permanent arrangement in the church, so that it cannot be urged for the monastic system. Ellicott renders it because of the impending distress, and finds the doubled construction, I think it is good and then I say I think it is good, strikingly characteristic of a writing taken down from dictation. Robertson takes the participle as standing on or present, and thinks Paul probably has in mind the calamities Jesus said would precede his coming.

Calvin, following ancient manuscripts, makes it one proposition rather than a repetition: celibacy is expedient on account of the necessity with which the saints are always harassed. Wesley narrows the inference sharply — the distress is urged no more for celibacy than for marriage, but for a man's not seeking to alter his state, whatever it be, but making the best of it. Lightfoot sets out the two questions the Corinthians had put by letter, and wonders how a scruple about single life could arise among Jewish believers at all.
27:
All of them read the pair of questions as an application of the counsel just given, and all take the first as addressed to men already married. Gill takes the bond of a promise, an espousal or a consummated marriage, the last a tie dissolved only by death, saving adultery and wilful desertion; it binds mutually, the husband to live chastely and provide, the wife to live in like manner and submit. Clarke notes simply that the marriage contract was considered in the light of a bond. Robertson parses the perfect passive and takes the imperative as a present prohibition, do not be seeking release. Calvin makes the clause a restriction on the commendation of celibacy, lest anyone hearing that praise despise marriage, forgetting his own necessity; Paul is not merely forbidding the breaking up of the connection but repressing the dislikes that creep in, that every man may live with his wife willingly and cheerfully.

The second question they will not let be read as divorce. Barnes says it should have been rendered free from a wife, or art thou single, and does not imply the person had ever been married, though it may cover those separated by a wife's death; there is no need to suppose Paul means divorced men, and he cites Grotius, Schleusner and Doddridge for it. Ellicott agrees that being loosed does not mean a separation after marriage but simply unmarried, and calls the whole verse an explanation and re-assertion of the words just before. Robertson includes bachelors as well as widowers under the participle, and notes that Paul urges this only because of the present necessity, not as his opinion for all men at all times, and gives the noblest view of marriage in the letter to the Ephesians; whether he held to it later we do not know. Calvin likewise takes the second clause with a reservation, since the apostle does not allow to all the choice of perpetual celibacy but only to those to whom it is given, and warns that no one under no necessity should rashly ensnare himself, for liberty ought not to be lightly thrown away.

On the concession that follows, Gill insists the apostle is not dissuading from marriage as sinful or criminal, only advising abstinence under present circumstances, and that what is said of the man holds equally of the virgin. Barnes says the counsel is mere advice, to be observed or not, and extends it: in persecution, or where a man is poor, or already supports a dependent mother and sisters, or where family cares would consume the time he might give to a missionary life, the same wisdom holds. Clarke suspects a target, since among the many sects at Corinth there were probably those who forbade to marry and who may have maintained other doctrines of devils besides. Calvin sees a scruple being removed, that a man might think he tempted God by binding himself willingly; he holds that virgins and widows are made equal here, not the one argued from the other, and recalls that second marriages among the ancients carried a mark of reproach, matrons content with one being honoured with a chaplet of chastity.

Ellicott takes the verbs as past and thinks a particular case from the Corinthian letter stands behind them, and reads the closing words not as a refusal to describe their troubles but as the apostle's whole motive in advising: my desire is to spare you them. Barnes reads it the other way, that he will not dwell on a melancholy theme. Clarke agrees that the evil is coming but the caution will not be pressed as too heavy a cross; Wesley, that he speaks as little and as tenderly as possible; Robertson takes the verb as possibly conative, I am trying to spare you.
29:
What the shortened time means divides them along a clean line. Gill offers both readings without choosing: either the time of life is short and it is but a little while to the end of the world, so that the single are more at leisure for spiritual good; or the apostle is still enlarging on the present distress, the time being contracted and full of anguish. Calvin takes it of human life, frail and of short duration, and will not have us entangled by it. Barnes explains the word as applied to furling a sail, reducing it into a narrow compass, and allows that the time may have been contracted by their impending trials, but insists it is always equally true that time is short, and no plan of life should be adopted that does not contemplate it. Clarke makes it historical: the persecutions are at the door, and even then Nero was plotting those with which he devastated the Church; he quotes Horace on the pleasing consort and the lands that must be left, and answers that poor heathenism gave but cold comfort in such circumstances. Robertson parses the perfect periphrastic, finds the verb in the papyri for curtailing expenses, reports that Calvin takes it of the shortness of life, but judges that Paul pictures the foreshortening of opportunity because of the possible nearness of the second coming, though in Philippians he faces death as his fate while still looking for it.

Ellicott alone makes the point a matter of principle and defends it. The words do not reiterate what has been said but begin a solemn warning, that whether or not they apply it to marriage it is of vast importance for regulating all life, that men should live ever expecting the return of the Lord. He will not have this thought a deduction from a mistaken belief that the Advent was close at hand: Christ himself taught it, warning men against living carelessly because they thought the Lord delayed his coming, and bidding them watch as servants for a master's unexpected return. Wesley draws the same practical force, that those who have wives should be as serious, zealous and dead to the world as if they had none, and marks how easily the apostle slides from everything else to the one thing needful.

On the weeping Gill denies that any stoical apathy is established or that a man should show no concern, directing instead to a moderate use of sorrow that will not divert him from piety. Barnes says the same more warmly: human nature cannot but feel when persecuted or bereaved, but religion pours oil on the agitated waves and lights up a smile in the midst of tears, and Christ himself sweat great drops of blood while Christians often weep. Clarke sets it in the coming confusion, when private sorrows and joys will be absorbed in weightier public evils, though a man should still buy and sell as usual, since persecution or death will soon level the propertied with the rest. Wesley glosses each clause in a phrase — sorrowful yet always rejoicing, joy tempered with godly fear, stewards not proprietors — and Robertson says all earthly relations should hang loosely about us.

On the last pair Calvin, Robertson and Ellicott all press the compound verb toward excess rather than crime. Calvin makes it using too much, directing us to a sober use of things that will not retard our course; Robertson renders it to use up, on the papyri; Ellicott warns against bondage to things in themselves right and good. Barnes takes the passing form from the shifting scenes of the drama, Calvin from a curtain drawn up on a new appearance, Robertson from a moving panorama; Gill bids the affluent use their plenty temperately. Clarke suspects the world here means the Jewish state and polity, whose destruction was then at hand.
32:
Gill and Barnes take the wish for freedom from care as a further reason for the advice, the married state being full of distracting cares about the sustenance of a family, so that the single are more at leisure for the service of God. Barnes glosses the word as anxiety or solicitude, such attention to this life as takes the thoughts off heavenly objects, and says Paul's own example showed what an unmarried man could give the Redeemer's kingdom. Robertson warns that this is the ideal state, since even the unmarried let the cares of the world choke the word. Clarke turns it into counsel about providence — though these things will shortly come to pass, do not be anxious, since every occurrence is under God's management — and quotes Byrom on running one's course of duty with a patient mind. Wesley adds his usual condition: the unmarried man cares only for the Lord's things if he understands and uses his advantage.

Calvin explains why the apostle returns so often to commend celibacy: he saw the burdens of matrimony were far from light, and those who resolve to marry do well to be forewarned, since many promise themselves unmixed honey and, disappointed, are cast down by the slightest mishap. He refuses the inference that the married are strangers to the kingdom: the apostle speaks only of a portion of the thoughts, as if to say they have one eye directed to the Lord but the other to their wife, marriage being a burden under which a pious mind does not move Godward so readily. These evils, he insists, do not belong to marriage but proceed from the depravity of men, and he rejects Jerome's calumnies. Barnes is franker: a man may be so anxious to gratify his wife that his affections are taken off the Lord, or his time for secret prayer consumed. Clarke draws the contrast to the married man's credit: the single man is an atom in society, the married man a small community in himself, living for himself and the public, and both state and Church depend upon him.

The clause about the wife and the virgin is textually vexed. Gill reports that the word rendered there is difference stands in some copies at the end of the previous verse, where the Vulgate and Ethiopic render it and is divided, of the married man whose mind is split between the Lord and his wife, though he follows the received reading. Robertson calls the text almost hopelessly uncertain, gives Westcott and Hort's arrangement by which the widow and the virgin are each anxious for the things of the Lord, and observes that the manuscripts vary at every point. Clarke finds such a profusion of readings that he refers the reader to Griesbach. Calvin adds that not all virgins and widows act this part, only that the opportunity is there, and turns sharply on the celibacy of monks and nuns; Barnes suggests the body is named in the woman's case because her temptation lies chiefly there; Wesley calls it the standing advantage of a single life, and asks who makes suitable use of it.

On the closing disclaimer the images multiply. Barnes takes the word for a cord and compares the yoke. Clarke sees an allusion to the Retiarius with his casting net, or to the Persian camand, a silken cord with a loop that tightens as it is pulled — he has one lying before him. Robertson calls it a slip-knot for lassoing animals. Ellicott renders the aim as comeliness and waiting on the Lord uncumbered, as Martha was cumbered; Wesley explains the word as sitting close by in a good posture to hear, as Mary sat at Jesus' feet. Calvin commends the apostle's moderation in pointing out what is most advantageous without imposing necessity, and Gill agrees that all was by way of advice.
36:
Nearly all take these verses of a father disposing of a daughter. Gill notes that some understand a man betrothed to a virgin who delays the marriage, but prefers a parent or guardian. Henry supplies the social fact behind the case: in that age, especially among the Jews, it was a disgrace for a woman to remain unmarried past a certain age, raising a suspicion against her reputation. Barnes draws the consequence, that a father's authority might involve his daughter in shame, and where it would, prohibiting her marriage would be wrong. Ellicott reads the uncomely behaviour as exposing her to temptation by withholding consent, and denies that the permission leaves the man indifferent: he is implied to think he ought to consent, and Paul bids him do what he so wills without fear. Robertson supposes the Corinthians had asked about a father's duty toward a daughter old enough to marry, and notes that Roman and Greek fathers controlled that, quoting Hermione — my marriage is my father's care. Calvin sees parents left in doubt by the praises of celibacy, wondering whether it were kind to involve their children in such miseries, and answers that they should consult a child's good as a free man consults his own.

Clarke alone lays out the alternatives, three of them. The first is the common one, that a father who had devoted his daughter to perpetual virginity, finding she had fixed her affections and was past her prime, might alter his purpose without sin. The second refers the passage to young women dedicated to God and called virgins in the primitive Church, circumstances arising that made breaking such a vow necessary. The third, held by Locke and Whitby, denies that the word means a virgin at all and takes it of the state of virginity, in a man as much as a woman, so that what is kept is the man's own purpose of it; the conditions fit only this, Whitby argues, since all turns on the purpose of his own heart and his power over his own will, whereas keeping a daughter unmarried would depend on her necessity, not his. Clarke cites Phavorinus, that he is a virgin who gives himself up to the Lord, renouncing matrimony.

On standing steadfast the weight falls on deliberation. Calvin warns that the steadfast purpose is not the monkish resolution, a binding over to perpetual servitude, but a thoroughly matured one, since men contrive schemes they regret the next day; and many bring obstinacy to their deliberations rather than reason, saying it is enough that such is their will, without considering what is in their power. Barnes opposes the phrase to a vacillating disposition, the freedom meaning that no engagement intervenes. Ellicott holds the previous verse strictly to cases where refusing consent would do positive harm. Robertson takes it of the daughter who does not wish to marry, her father agreeing. Wesley glosses the power over one's own will as what would otherwise incline a man to desire his family's increase.

Ellicott makes a fine point of the tenses in the summary, the present for the man who gives in marriage as though the good began and ended there, the future for the man who does not, the good continuing while she remains; the passage contrasts degrees of expediency, not right and wrong, and no advice at all is given the maiden herself. Calvin allows the preference only under the exception already made: if the power to abstain is wanting in the daughter, the father acts an exceedingly bad part and is no longer a father but a cruel tyrant. Gill lists what the marriage secures — her chastity, his credit, the prevention of evils. Barnes, Wesley and Robertson attach the preference to the circumstances, and Robertson adds that Paul leaves the whole problem an open question, to be settled case by case.
39:
Gill and Henry take the closing words as settled law: the wife is bound to her husband by the law of marriage during his life, and the bond is dissolved only by death, excepting adultery and wilful desertion. Henry infers that the marriage contract is for life and death only can annul it, but that it is certain from this passage that second marriages are not unlawful, since otherwise the widow could not be at liberty to marry whom she pleased at all. Robertson calls this the ideal, pertinent still when husbands meet their former wives; there is a screw loose somewhere. He treats the remarriage of widows as an addendum, discussed again in the letter to Timothy where younger widows are advised to marry. Clarke suspects another Corinthian question behind it, whether a woman may remarry whose husband is dead or has abandoned her. Calvin explains why women needed a separate word: the apostle had spoken indiscriminately of husbands and wives, but since wives, from the modesty of their sex, might seem to have less liberty, he adds special directions, teaching that women are no less free than men to marry again on becoming widows.

Calvin then turns the point into a protest. Those who desired a second marriage were branded with intemperance, and the chaplet of chastity was given to slight them by honouring those content with one; worse, that opinion became prevalent among Christians, so that second marriages had no blessing pronounced upon them and some Councils forbade the clergy to attend them. Such tyranny the Apostle condemns, declaring that no hindrance ought to be thrown in the way of widows marrying.

The limitation they read as confining her choice to a believer. Barnes takes it of a Christian only, and gives his reasons: they could have no sympathy on the most important of all subjects; a widow marrying a heathen would show she had not as deep a conviction of her religion as she ought; the precepts to be separate and unconformed to the world could not be obeyed if she chose such society for life; and she would hinder her usefulness under one with no respect for her faith. Clarke goes beyond Christian profession and would have her marry not merely a genuine Christian but one of her own religious sentiments, since much of domestic peace depends on it. Wesley calls it a standing direction of the utmost importance; Robertson says every marriage ought to be in the Lord. Henry turns it into counsel for all such choices: in our change of conditions we should have an eye to God, and marriages have his blessing only when persons are guided by his fear and laws and depend on his providence.

Gill explains the happiness as of this life, not another, the widow being freer from care and more at leisure to serve the Lord, second marriages often proving more disagreeable than the first. Calvin denies that widowhood is itself a virtue and grounds the preference on its freedom from distraction. Clarke enters the sharpest caveat in the chapter: the words must be held to the present distress, since a woman who had tried both states could best tell which suited her, and the apostle could say nothing of a widow's future except by revelation; multitudes are happier married, and many widows happier in a second marriage than the first. On the last clause Barnes weighs the verb and denies, against Macknight, that it expresses absolute certainty, allowing a strong persuasion or the best judgment the mind can form, and suspects an allusion to the Corinthian teachers' claims to inspiration. Wesley reads it the opposite way, as the strongest certainty with a reproof of them for questioning it; Calvin hears irony against the false apostles who boasted of the Spirit to derogate from Paul; Robertson has him leave each one to decide.
